problem:
What is the smallest possible distance between the points $(4x,\,-x)$ and $(5,\,-1),$ where $x$ is a real number? Do not round the answer.

The smallest possible distance is
{{field-1}}.
worked_solution:
First, let's compute the *squared* distance $S(x)$ between the two points. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}S(x) & ={((4x)-5)}^{2}+{((-x)-(-1))}^{2} \\  & =(4x-5)^{2}+(-x+1)^{2} \\  & =(16{x}^{2}-40x+25)+({x}^{2}-2x+1) \\  & =17{x}^{2}-42x+26.\end{aligned}
$$

Since we want to minimize $S,$ we compute the derivative ${S}^{′}(x).$ This gives

$$
{S}^{′}(x)=34x-42.
$$

The stationary points of $S(x)$ are the points where the derivative ${S}^{′}(x)=0.$ Solving this equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}^{′}(x) & =0 \\ 34x-42 & =0 \\ x & =\frac{21}{17}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can see that ${S}^{″}\,(\frac{21}{17})=34>0.$

So, the squared distance (and therefore the actual distance) reaches a minimum when $x=\frac{21}{17}.$ 

Since $S(x)$ gives the squared distance between the two points, the actual distance $d$ between the two points when $x=\frac{21}{17}$ is given by

$$
d=\sqrt{S\,(\frac{21}{17})}.
$$

Computing this quantity, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =\sqrt{S\,(\frac{21}{17})} \\  & =\sqrt{17{(\frac{21}{17})}^{2}-42(\frac{21}{17})+26} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{441}{17}-\frac{882}{17}+26} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{1}{17}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{17}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{17}}{17}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the smallest possible distance between the points $(4x,\,-x)$ and $(5,\,-1)$ is $\frac{\sqrt{17}}{17}.$
